sections.name: File setup, AppModule (part 1)
sections.title: Settings, logging, and shared modules
sections.what: Loads settings from the environment files, sets up request logging with three fields hidden, and loads the shared infrastructure modules for the database, Redis, storage, and security.
sections.why: Likely reason: every feature needs the settings and the logs. The hidden fields are the login header and the password and code fields in request bodies.
sections.watch_out: Only three fields are hidden, so other personal data can still show up in logs.

sections.name: File setup, AppModule (part 2)
sections.title: Feature modules list
sections.what: Lists the feature areas of the API: login, users, documents, reminders, health, family, sharing, chat, notifications, timeline, consent, and compliance.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. Each area is a separate feature group, but the order is not explained.
sections.watch_out: A new feature area is active only after it is added to this list.

summary: The root setup that loads settings, configures logging, and connects every feature module of the API.
purpose: Assembles the whole API from its parts so that all features start together.
why: The header states that it composes the domain modules with DDD boundaries, meaning each feature area is kept separate.
how: 1) Load settings from .env.local, then .env. 2) Configure request logging, with pretty output only outside production and when enabled. 3) Load the shared common and security modules. 4) Load each feature module in a list.
inputs: NODE_ENV, USE_PINO_PRETTY, LOG_LEVEL, and the environment files.
outputs: A running application with every feature module registered.
risks: The log redaction list hides only three fields: the authorization header, the password in the body, and the one-time code in the body. Other personal data could still appear in logs. A feature module that is missing from the list will not be loaded.
debug: If an endpoint returns not found, check that its module is in the list. If sensitive data appears in logs, compare the redaction list with the data being logged. If a setting is ignored, check the environment file names.
